June 15, 2026 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
200 Independence Avenue, SW  
Washington, DC 20201 
 
Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov  
 
Re: Request for Information on Prior Authorization Requirements for Laboratory 
Tests and DMEPOS Items [CMS-0062-P] 
 
Dear Dr. Oz:  
On behalf of the National Society of Genetic Counselors (NSGC), thank you for the 
opportunity to respond to the Request for Information on prior authorization for 
laboratory tests contained in the proposed rule on Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs (CMS-0062-P). NSGC is the leading voice of genetic 
counselors, advocating for their various roles, advancing the practice of genetic 
counseling, and fostering collaboration, education, and research to ensure equitable 
access to genomic healthcare. With nearly 200,000 genetic tests on the clinical global 
market and 10 new tests introduced every day, genetic counselors are uniquely 
positioned to provide CMS with subject matter expertise on the clinical value of 
appropriate, medically necessary genetic tests and the impact that prior authorization 
requirements have on patient access to those tests. 
Our responses to select questions from the request for information are below.  
1. How do prior authorization requirements for laboratory tests currently 
impact patient care and health care provider burden? 
With respect to genetic testing, unjustified prior authorization requirements have been 
found to cause measurable patient harm by reducing or delaying access to clinically 
indicated tests that would otherwise yield actionable diagnoses. In a study of over 3,300 
genetic test prior authorization requests for pediatric Medicaid patients in Texas, 
unfavorable prior authorization outcomes reduced the likelihood that testing was 
completed (37.8% completion after denial versus 74.2% after approval), andâ€”
counterintuitivelyâ€”tests completed after denial had significantly higher diagnostic yields 
than those with favorable outcomes (26.7% versus 18.7%), demonstrating that 
coverage criteria were filtering out the very tests most likely to produce diagnoses.1 A 
 
1 Streff, Haley, et al. "Access to Clinically Indicated Genetic Tests for Pediatric Patients with Medicaid: 
Evidence from Outpatient Genetics Clinics in Texas." Genetics in Medicine, vol. 25, 2023, p. 100350, 
doi:10.1016/j.gim.2022.11.018. PMID 36547467 
 
separate study among 801 pediatric patients denied clinical genetic testing revealed 
54% were later found through research testing to have at least one diagnostic or 
candidate genetic finding, and 50% of those with confirmed diagnostic findings 
experienced immediate changes in medical management2â€”demonstrating that prior 
authorization requirements are not merely administrative inconveniences but may result 
in missed diagnoses and delayed changes in treatment that constitute concrete, 
measurable patient harm.  
Regarding provider burden, unneeded prior authorization for genetic tests imposes 
disproportionate administrative costs on genetic counselors, who lack Medicare provider 
status and therefore receive no reimbursement from CMS for the time they spend on 
documentation, appeals, and payer communications. CPT code 96041, evaluated and 
approved for use beginning in January 2025, reflects the change in practice brought 
about by rising administrative burden on genetic counselors, recognizing that 54% of 
these clinicians now are supported by â€œgenetic counselor assistantsâ€ to complete this 
work.3 This procedure code includes valuation of the time spent by genetic counselor 
assistants on the date of service to prepare the necessary documentation for many 
genetic testing prior authorization requests and subsequently submit that prior 
authorization request to ensure patients can undergo specimen collection in a timely 
manner. While covered by some commercial and state payors, CPT code 96041 is not 
covered by CMS. This genetic counseling services reimbursement gap, when analyzed 
together with the data that clinically unnecessary prior authorization reduces access to 
appropriate testing, results in an administrative burden and service cost increase with 
no discernable benefit to patients or payors. 
Research shows that prior authorization reviewers at insurers consistently lack genetics 
expertise, requiring extensive genetic counselor time to explain clinical rationale.4 
Because genetic counselors lack Medicare provider status, their time spent on prior 
authorization documentation, appeals, and payer communications generates no 
reimbursement when seeing traditional Medicare beneficiaries. In a recent survey of 
genetic counselors serving the Medicaid population, most respondents reported 
absorbing Medicaid navigation responsibilities without adequate institutional support or 
training, exacerbating provider burden.5   
 
2 Zion, Tricia N., et al. "Insurance Denials and Diagnostic Rates in a Pediatric Genomic Research 
Cohort." Genetics in Medicine, vol. 25, no. 5, 2023, p. 100020, doi:10.1016/j.gim.2023.100020. 
3 January 2024 AMA/Specialty Society RVS Update Committee (RUC) meeting minutes reporting 
â€œGenetic Counseling Services,â€  https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/jan-2024-ruc-meeting-minutes.pdf  
4 Lin, Grace A., et al. "Influence of Payer Coverage and Out-of-Pocket Costs on Ordering of Next-
Generation Sequencing Panel Tests for Hereditary Cancer in Diverse Settings." Journal of Genetic 
Counseling, vol. 31, no. 1, 2022, pp. 130â€“139, doi:10.1002/jgc4.1459. PMID 34231930. 
5 Lockhart, Jessica, et al. "Assessing Genetic Counselors' Knowledge of Medicaid Access and Service 
Delivery." NSGC 44th Annual Conference Abstracts. Journal of Genetic Counseling, 2026. National 
Society of Genetic Counselors (NSGC) 44th Annual Conference, 7â€“10 Nov. 2025, Seattle, WA. 
 
4. What impacts have laboratory benefit managers (LBMs) had in facilitating 
prior authorization processes, regulating access, and controlling payment 
for laboratory services? 
According to a policy analysis funded by the National Institutes of Health, by design, 
LBMs impose mandatory prior authorization requirements for all genetic tests 
regardless of clinical indication. LBMs were found to require ordering clinicians rather 
than laboratories to provide documentation and may create conflicts of interest when 
owned by a laboratory or insurer.6 While it is challenging to have full transparency of 
their contractual and financial incentive structures, reporting found an association with 
LBMs and denials.7 In Arkansasâ€”the only state requiring public disclosure of LBM 
denial ratesâ€”data showed one LBM denied nearly 20% of prior authorization requests 
versus approximately 7% for Medicare Advantage plans generally.8  
Additionally, NSGCâ€™s own research on payer coverage policies in early 2025 revealed 
that when payers transition to LBM-managed policies, coverage gaps for genetic 
counseling services can emerge. Prior to transitioning to an LBM, NSGC found some 
health plansâ€™ original genetic testing policies specifically provided coverage guidance on 
genetic counseling as well. However, the LBM-replacement policies failed to address 
genetic counseling coverage, such as for CPT code 96041. When discussing these 
issues with two LBMs, NSGC learned the LBMâ€™s â€œsoleâ€ focus is on clinical criteria 
associated with each clinical category of test and applicable CPT codes that the 
individual health plan delegates to it for review. Services addressed in a legacy policy 
such as genetic counseling or any other professional service and their applicable billing 
codes are not delegated to the LBM. This resulted in a coordination failure: the health 
plansâ€™ new policies only address genetic testing and no longer contain an explicit policy 
for genetic counseling services. A lapse in properly recognizing the CPT code 96041 
can cause avoidable administrative issues for genetic counselors, patients, plans, and 
the LBM and ultimately add to dissatisfaction with the health plan. A health planâ€™s failure 
to address all aspects of their legacy policies like genetic counseling services can lead 
to this coordination problem.     
5. What opportunities for process improvement exist for prior authorization 
requirements? 
 
6 Phillips, Kathryn A., and Patricia A. Deverka. "The Emerging Use by Commercial Payers of Third-Party 
Lab Benefit Managers for Genetic Testing." Health Affairs Forefront, 23 Oct. 2019, 
doi:10.1377/hblog20191021.563154. 
7 Miller, T. Christian, Patrick Rucker, and David Armstrong. "'Not Medically Necessary': Inside the 
Company Helping America's Biggest Health Insurers Deny Coverage for Care." ProPublica and The 
Capitol Forum, 24 Oct. 2024, www.propublica.org/article/evicore-health-insurance-denials-cigna-
unitedhealthcare-aetna-prior-authorizations.  
8 Ibid. 
 
NSGC requests CMS consider evidence showing process improvements tied to genetic 
counselor involvement in test order review as an evidence-based alternative to blunt the 
potential harms from unjustified prior authorization requirements for genetic tests. A 
2025 scoping review of 51 studies spanning multiple payer types found that genetic 
counselor involvement in test order review reduced inappropriate ordering, improved 
diagnostic rates, generated economic efficiencies, and even improved non-genetics 
providersâ€™ ordering practices.9 This scoping review is reinforced by other studies. At the 
Cleveland Clinic, a genetic counselor-gated ordering initiative saved $1,531,913 over 
two years through reduced inappropriate testing.10 In a separate study at an academic 
medical center, patients who met with a genetic counselor had a 31-fold greater odds of 
receiving eligibility-appropriate genetic testing.11  
By the same token, embedding genetic counselors in a payerâ€™s policy team is another 
needed process improvement. One study found genetic counselors embedded in a 
payer policy team initiated 115 of 138 policy actions across 50 genetic testing policies 
over two years, continuously aligning coverage with evolving clinical guidelines. 
Specifically, aligning policies with current literature and guidelines included updating 
hereditary cancer policies each time NCCN guidelines were revised, aligning 
pharmacogenomics policy with CPIC guidelines, and adding rapid whole genome 
sequencing criteria.12 These data demonstrate that genetic counselor involvement 
achieves the cost-containment and utilization management outcomes that prior 
authorization systems may be designed for but fail to deliver in practice, as these 
positive outcomes happen at the point of care, without creating barriers to access or 
imposing administrative burden on providers and patients.     
To realize the full potential of appropriate ordering at the point of care, NSGC 
recommends that CMS support the bipartisan Access to Genetic Counselor Services 
Act to establish Medicare recognition of genetic counselors, which would create a 
reimbursable pre-test counseling pathway providing both a program integrity safeguard 
and improved quality of care for Medicare beneficiaries.  We also encourage CMS to 
consider pilot programs examining the effect of pre-test genetic counseling on 
downstream utilization and cost.  
 
9 Cook, Courtney B., Alison Pistawka, and Alison M. Elliott. "The Impact of Genetic Counselor 
Involvement in Genetic and Genomic Test Order Review: A Scoping Review." Genetics in Medicine, vol. 
27, no. 3, 2025, p. 101354, doi:10.1016/j.gim.2025.101354. PMID 39807624. 
10 Riley, Jacquelyn D., et al. "Improving Molecular Genetic Test Utilization through Order Restriction, Test 
Review, and Guidance." Journal of Molecular Diagnostics, vol. 17, no. 3, 2015, pp. 225â€“229, 
doi:10.1016/j.jmoldx.2015.01.003. PMID 25732008. 
11 Erali, R.A., et al. "Pivotal Role of Genetic Counselors in the Uptake of Germline Genetic Testing in 
Non-Metastatic Breast Cancer and the Impact of Testing on Surgical Decision Making." The American 
Surgeon, vol. 89, Dec. 2023, doi:10.1177/00031348231175097. 
12 Baxter, Adrianne, et al. "Insurance Payor Policy for Genetic Testing: Impact of Genetic Counselors as 
Part of the Team." NSGC 44th Annual Conference Abstracts. Journal of Genetic Counseling, 2026. 
National Society of Genetic Counselors 44th Annual Conference, 7â€“10 Nov. 2025, Seattle, WA. 
 
7. and 8. What other issues exist regarding prior authorization processes for 
laboratory tests and DMEPOS items that technology is not 
currently addressing? and How do the issues associated with prior 
authorization impact the health care workforce and retention of 
skilled health care professionals? 
NSGC wishes to answer these two questions together as they relate to a workforce 
sustainability problem for achieving high quality genetic testing orders, correct 
diagnoses, and timely treatments, that prior authorization technology alone cannot 
solve. Genetic counselors are clinicians with specialized graduate-level training in 
medical genetics and counseling, certified by the American Board of Genetic 
Counseling or the American Board of Medical Genetics and Genomics, with 
approximately 7,000 certified practitioners in the United States. In clinical practice, 
genetic counselors perform functions directly relevant to appropriate test utilization and 
program integrity: clinical assessment to determine whether genetic testing is clinically 
indicated, test selection from among nearly 200,000 options, informed consent, result 
interpretation, and variant management. 
Despite this critical role, as noted above, genetic counselors are not currently 
recognized as independent Medicare providers and cannot bill Medicare directly for 
their services. This creates two undesirable outcomes: either Medicare patients do not 
receive genetic counselor services at all or, perhaps less common, genetic counselors 
spend significant time on prior authorization documentation, appeals, and payer 
communications for Medicare beneficiaries, yet this work generates no reimbursement 
because Medicare does not cover their services. Prior authorization technology 
aloneâ€”whether an electronic prior authorization API or FHIR-based 
interoperability standardâ€”will never address the fundamental issue that genetic 
counselors, the very clinicians best qualified to evaluate genetic test 
appropriateness and counsel patients appropriately in often challenging 
circumstances, are excluded from the Medicare reimbursement pathway. In 
addition, while technology-based solutions for streamlining prior authorization are 
welcome, making the process of submitting prior authorization requests faster through 
electronic APIs does not address a fundamental knowledge gap on the reviewer side as 
evidenced by the above-referenced Lin study. Genetic counselor involvement in test 
order review at the point of care, as an alternative or supplement to payer-side prior 
authorization, addresses the root cause by ensuring that clinically appropriate tests are 
ordered at the right place and at the right time. 
NSGC stands ready to partner with CMS to develop evidentiary records, policy 
frameworks, and practical tools related to genetic testing utilization management, and 
we welcome the opportunity to serve as a resource on these issues. If you have any 
questions, please do not hesitate to contact Meghan Carey at mcarey@nsgc.org. 
 
 
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
Carrie Haverty, MS, CGC 
NSGC President
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** National Society of Genetic Counselors (NSGC); signed by Carrie Haverty, MS, CGC, NSGC President.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association; Healthcare Provider representative.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** NSGC represents genetic counselors and describes genetic counselors as clinicians with graduate-level training in medical genetics and counseling, certified by the American Board of Genetic Counseling or the American Board of Medical Genetics and Genomics.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

NSGC argues that prior authorization requirements for genetic laboratory testing can cause measurable patient harm, impose unreimbursed burden on genetic counselors, and fail when reviewers lack genetics expertise. It recommends using genetic counselor involvement in test-order review and payer policy development as a better utilization-management strategy, while supporting Medicare recognition of genetic counselors and pilots on pre-test counseling effects.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** GENERAL; GENERAL/RFIs on laboratory tests; indirectly relevant to electronic PA technology but not tied to a specific proposed FHIR/NCPDP provision.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None specifically cited.
- **Standards referenced:** CPT code 96041; electronic prior authorization APIs; FHIR-based interoperability standards; NCCN guidelines; CPIC guidelines.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Patient harm from genetic test prior authorization**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Oppose
- **Rationale:** NSGC cites studies showing denials reduce testing completion and may block tests with high diagnostic yield, leading to missed diagnoses and delayed treatment changes.
- **Specific request:** CMS should recognize the clinical harm from unjustified genetic testing PA and consider alternatives that do not delay clinically indicated testing.

**Topic 2: Administrative burden and Medicare reimbursement gap**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Genetic counselors spend time on documentation, appeals, and payer communications but lack Medicare provider status and cannot bill CMS for this work. CPT code 96041 reflects this administrative work in other payer contexts but is not covered by CMS.
- **Specific request:** CMS should support the Access to Genetic Counselor Services Act to establish Medicare recognition and reimbursement for genetic counselors.

**Topic 3: Laboratory Benefit Managers and coverage coordination**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** NSGC states LBMs can impose mandatory PA for all genetic tests, require ordering clinicians to submit documentation, create conflicts of interest, and cause coverage gaps when genetic counseling services are omitted from replacement policies.
- **Specific request:** CMS should consider LBM transparency, denial patterns, conflicts of interest, and coordination failures affecting services such as CPT code 96041.

**Topic 4: Genetic counselor involvement as process improvement**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** NSGC cites evidence that genetic counselor involvement reduces inappropriate ordering, improves diagnostic rates, creates economic efficiencies, improves provider ordering practices, and keeps payer policies aligned with current clinical guidelines.
- **Specific request:** CMS should promote genetic counselor test-order review, embedded genetic counselor roles in payer policy teams, and pilot programs evaluating pre-test counseling effects on utilization and cost.

**Topic 5: Limits of technology-only prior authorization solutions**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** NSGC welcomes technology that streamlines PA submission but argues that APIs or FHIR-based standards cannot solve reviewer knowledge gaps or the lack of Medicare reimbursement for qualified genetic counselors.
- **Specific request:** CMS should pair technology solutions with workforce and reimbursement reforms that enable genetic counselors to evaluate test appropriateness at the point of care.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S66-S82:** NSGC responds to the general RFI questions on laboratory tests, including patient-care impact, provider burden, LBMs, process improvements, technology gaps, and workforce effects. The response emphasizes genetic testing and genetic counselor involvement rather than the drug PA API provisions.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Treat unjustified prior authorization for genetic tests as a source of measurable patient harm.
2. Support the Access to Genetic Counselor Services Act to recognize genetic counselors as Medicare providers.
3. Consider pilot programs examining pre-test genetic counseling effects on downstream utilization and cost.
4. Promote genetic counselor involvement in genetic test-order review as an evidence-based utilization-management alternative.
5. Encourage payer policy teams to include genetic counselors so genetic testing policies remain aligned with current evidence and guidelines.
6. Improve transparency and oversight of LBMs, including denial rates, ownership incentives, and effects on related genetic counseling coverage.
7. Ensure technology solutions do not substitute for subject-matter expertise in genetic testing review.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Denial or delay of clinically indicated genetic testing; payer reviewer lack of genetics expertise; unreimbursed genetic counselor administrative work; LBM denial and coordination problems; Medicare nonrecognition of genetic counselors.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Missed diagnoses, delayed changes in medical management, reduced test completion, inappropriate denial of high-yield testing, administrative dissatisfaction, and weakened access to genomic healthcare.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Lack of Medicare provider status, no CMS coverage for CPT code 96041, inadequate payer genetics expertise, opaque LBM incentives, fragmented policies, and technology solutions that do not address workforce or reviewer knowledge gaps.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Nearly 200,000 genetic tests on the clinical global market; 10 new tests introduced daily; in a Texas pediatric Medicaid study, test completion was 37.8% after denial versus 74.2% after approval, and diagnostic yield was 26.7% after denial versus 18.7% after favorable outcomes; among 801 pediatric patients denied testing, 54% later had diagnostic or candidate findings and 50% of confirmed findings led to immediate management changes; approximately 7,000 certified genetic counselors in the United States; one LBM reportedly denied nearly 20% of PA requests compared with about 7% for MA plans generally.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Streff et al.; Zion et al.; AMA RUC materials for CPT 96041; Lin et al.; Lockhart et al.; Phillips and Deverka; ProPublica/Capitol Forum reporting; Cook et al.; Riley et al.; Erali et al.; Baxter et al.
- **Examples provided:** Cleveland Clinic genetic counselor-gated ordering saved $1,531,913 over two years; patients who met with a genetic counselor had 31-fold greater odds of receiving eligibility-appropriate testing; payer policy genetic counselors initiated 115 of 138 policy actions across 50 genetic testing policies.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Genetic counselors, patients needing genetic testing, pediatric Medicaid patients, Medicare beneficiaries, ordering clinicians, payers, LBMs, health plans, CMS, and genetic testing laboratories.
- **Economic implications:** Prior authorization creates unreimbursed administrative labor for genetic counselors and may not deliver cost-containment benefits. Genetic counselor-led review can reduce inappropriate testing and generate savings.
- **Technical feasibility:** Electronic PA APIs and FHIR-based standards may improve submission speed, but NSGC argues technology alone cannot resolve clinical appropriateness review or reimbursement gaps.
- **Patient care impact:** The comment presents prior authorization as a cause of missed or delayed diagnoses and delayed management changes, especially where genetic testing is clinically indicated.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Concerned
- **Tone:** Professional, evidence-based, and critical of current PA approaches
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "unjustified prior authorization requirements have been found to cause measurable patient harm" - Context: Frames NSGC’s central objection to genetic test PA.
2. "coverage criteria were filtering out the very tests most likely to produce diagnoses" - Context: Summarizes the pediatric Medicaid evidence cited by NSGC.
3. "prior authorization technology alone" - Context: Introduces NSGC’s argument that APIs cannot solve the underlying workforce and expertise problems.
4. "excluded from the Medicare reimbursement pathway" - Context: Describes the Medicare recognition gap for genetic counselors.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - NSGC discusses unreimbursed genetic counselor labor, CPT code 96041, administrative costs, and documented savings from genetic counselor-led test review.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - The comment focuses on documentation, appeals, payer communications, and Medicaid navigation burdens placed on genetic counselors.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - The comment links PA barriers to reduced access to genomic healthcare and cites Medicaid patient evidence.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - NSGC discusses electronic APIs and FHIR-based standards while explaining what technology cannot solve.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The central patient impact is reduced or delayed access to clinically indicated genetic tests.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment recommends genetic counselor involvement in payer policy teams and coordinated recognition of counseling services.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - NSGC raises transparency concerns about LBM denial rates, incentives, and policy replacement effects.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment addresses test-order review, policy development, documentation, appeals, and payer communications.
